subject: Computer Networking
title: Packet Switching Invented
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Packet Switching Invented.

hook.text: In 1961, Leonard Kleinrock proposed splitting data into small blocks that could each find their own way.

buildup.text: Circuit switching wasted bandwidth — the full line was reserved even during silence. Packets fixed that.

discovery.text: Paul Baran at RAND and Donald Davies at NPL independently developed packet switching in the early 1960s.

twist.text: The U.S. military funded Baran's work. They needed a network that could survive nuclear attack by rerouting packets.

climax.text: Packet switching became the foundation of ARPANET and eventually the entire internet.

punchline.text: One idea — split data into packets — created the modern internet.

quiz.question: Why was packet switching more efficient than circuit switching?
options: Bandwidth wasn't wasted on idle connections

details.summary: Packet switching, independently conceived by Paul Baran and Donald Davies in the 1960s, breaks data into small packets that travel independently through the network and reassemble at the destination.
details.whyItMatters: Packet switching is the single most important invention in networking history. It made the internet possible by enabling efficient, robust sharing of network capacity among millions of users.
takeaways: Data is broken into small packets that travel independently
Packets can take different routes and reassemble at the destination
Packet switching shares bandwidth far more efficiently than circuits

faq.question: Why is packet switching more efficient than circuit switching?
faq.answer: Circuit switching reserves a full path even during silence. Packet switching breaks data into small pieces that share the network with everyone else's packets. This statistical multiplexing means the same network can serve vastly more users because idle capacity is always available for others.

faq.question: How did Baran and Davies both invent packet switching?
faq.answer: They worked independently and did not know of each other's work. Baran at RAND was designing survivable military networks. Davies at the UK's National Physical Laboratory was optimizing computer communication. Their solutions converged on the same fundamental principle.
